extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry criticism; literary critics and readers learning close reading of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analysing and judging figurative language, sense, tone, and reader responses in poems; aimed at teaching close reading and practical criticism. Emphasises diagnosing reader errors and assessing whether poetic means serve poetic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most poetry needs several readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Most poetry needs several readings — in which its varied factors may fit themselves together — before it can be grasped. Readers who claim to dispense with this preliminary study, who think that all good poetry should come home to them in entirety at a first reading, hardly realise how clever they must be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat first impressions as provisional. Re-read to disentangle sense, metre, and tone; silence distracting features (e.g., verse-form) while resolving sense, then allow them to co-operate. Many misunderstandings arise from insufficient readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid careless 'intuitive' reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Careless, 'intuitive' reading—guess-work that claims to apprehend poetical sense at once—produces serious misreadings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on an immediate poetic 'intuition' to substitute for attention to literal sense and syntax. Test intuitive impressions by checking syntax and coherence; many protocol errors stem from intuitive leaps without verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prosaic 'over-literal' reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosaic, 'over-literal' reading—wrenching the sense free from the poem and reducing it to prose paraphrase—can equally misrepresent the poem's effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge poetic means by external prosaic standards (e.g., literal fact or strict logical coherence) unless those standards are relevant to the poem's aim. Beware the twin dangers of intuition and over-literal paraphrase (the 'Simplegades').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense and syntax in poetry remain crucial
rubrics_metrics.description: In most poetry the sense is as important as anything else; it is quite as subtle, and as dependent on the syntax, as in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend carefully to syntax when determining sense; misreading syntax often causes loss of poetic value. The poet's control of thought is ordinarily the chief means to control feeling; misreading sense loses much of the poem's worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic liberties permitted only when justified by aim
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may dissolve coherence or break facts and possibility if his other aims make the liberty worth while; nonsense is admissible in poetry if the effect justifies it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge such liberties by whether they achieve the poem's intended effect. When coherence is sacrificed, the critic must determine if the end (feeling, tone, imaginative effect) compensates for the loss of literal sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain the poem's aim before judging its means
rubrics_metrics.description: We have first to ascertain what the aim of the poem is. The aim (the mental condition which shaped the poem) is the sole justification of its means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the poem's intention(s) — which may be multiple or vague — before applying external standards. Misidentifying the intention will skew judgments of tone, figurative language, and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed metaphors must preserve efficacy of ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixtures in metaphors may work when the ingredients preserve their efficacy, but fail when such a fusion invites cancellation of the parts (notably 'fire and water' mixtures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse whether components of mixed imagery complement or cancel one another. Example: the 'sea/harp/lightning' passage shows when ingredients conflict (strings woven vs lightning) causing incoherence; a mixed metaphor is not automatically bad but mustn't create internal contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal coherence of figurative detail matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal inconsistencies in a figure (e.g., 'the sea may sound like an organ, but it never has the sound of a harp'; 'strings are not woven') break the coherence of sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify separate cracks in a figure's sense and ask whether they derive from a single justified liberty or are independent faults. Minor incoherences may be tolerable if the overall effect is achieved; flag multiple unconnected flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literalism (demanding scientific precision) is a misapplied standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Demanding that poetic language meet scientific or overly literal standards (e.g., chemistry-style precision) will condemn much good poetry; many readers mistake exaggeration for ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid applying irrelevant factual or technical standards when evaluating metaphor and hyperbole. Instead, ask whether the figurative choice realizes the poem's aim; use paraphrase and grammatical 'as if' reasoning cautiously to make sense of figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification: degrees, condensing power, and risks of overprojection
rubrics_metrics.description: Personification ranges from a momentary loan of a human attribute to projection of a complete spiritual being. It can be invaluable for condensation and vividness but becomes crippling if unjustifiably overdone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether personification economises expression (making hard things easy to describe) or overburdens the poem by projecting undue character. Check for appropriate degree: underdone personification may fail to convey an intended personality; overdone projection may empty the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation and economy by figurative devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensation and economy are often necessary in poetry so that emotional impulses do not dissipate; devices like personification can compendiously convey what prose would need diagrams to show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value images that achieve vivid, particular effects economically (e.g., 'slant your hand' to show shadow angle). Prefer compact, single-word movements that carry visual/affective load over verbose paraphrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of readers' prior influences and intertextual bias
rubrics_metrics.description: A reader's liking or dislike may be affected by acquaintance with other poets (e.g., Swinburne); previous exposure can lead to partiality or unconscious imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether enthusiasm derives from original engagement or from familiarity with source influences. Compare readers before and after exposure to influential poets; ask 'who fished the murex up?' to detect borrowed taste or obsessional echoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative criticism is fallacious if used simplistically
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguing that a poet is wrong simply because another poet (e.g., Shelley) did something differently is an over-simple and fallacious form of criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparisons only when the relevant conditions and intentions are carefully aligned. Recognise differences in intent and means; comparative judgment must examine whether similar ends are genuinely being pursued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone is a distinct and crucial dimension to judge
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone—the poet's attitude to listeners given what he has to say—is a distinct character in a poem and may decide its success; faults of tone (over-insistence, condescension) can ruin otherwise good poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether tone fits the subject-matter and the audience: does the poet overdo familiar thoughts, or does he find the right key? Consider historical manners and whether perceived rudeness or neglect of reader is justified by the poem's claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for period-specific codes and 'manners'
rubrics_metrics.description: Good manners and codes vary by period; what was appropriate in the eighteenth century may be poor taste in the twentieth, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place tone and manner in historical context before condemning them. Distinguish between fundamental manners (enduring sensibilities) and period codes (variable taste).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader obstacles: unfamiliar words, missing context, defective scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance, lack of acquaintance with words, absence of intellectual contexts, and defective scholarship can cause errors in apprehending sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between errors due to information gaps (fixable by reference works) and deeper misconceptions about how poetic language should be read. Teach students to check factual gaps but also to learn poetical senses that are not remedied by dictionaries alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close reading requires balancing fidelity to fact with recognition of poetic liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: All respectable poetry invites close reading; it encourages attention to its literal sense up to the point at which liberty can serve the aim of the poem better than fidelity to fact or strict coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reader's discretion to detect where liberty is productive. Quarrel with the poem's aim when necessary, but first ascertain the aim; judge means in light of that aim rather than by external factual or logical standards.
